title: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
summary: Specifies HKDF, a key derivation function built on HMAC. It can be used as a building block in many protocols and applications, taking some initial keying material and producing strong keys. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a protocol holds one secret value and needs many separate keys. HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function) turns that one value into any number of strong keys, in two short steps. Several IETF protocols already use it, and this RFC writes the method down so that new protocols can share it instead of inventing their own.

questions: how to derive keys with hmac
how does hkdf extract and expand work
should i use hkdf for passwords
what is the salt in hkdf
subtitle: A two-step recipe that turns one source of secret key material into as many strong keys as a protocol needs.

tldr.problem: Protocols often start with keying material that is not uniformly random, such as a shared Diffie-Hellman value, and need several cryptographically strong keys from it. Each protocol was defining its own way to do this.
tldr.mechanism: HKDF works in two steps. Extract uses HMAC to concentrate the input keying material into a fixed-length pseudorandom key, and Expand uses HMAC again to stretch that key into as many output octets as the protocol asks for.
tldr.outcome: It documents one general-purpose key derivation function to discourage a proliferation of mechanisms. It is not a call to change existing protocols, and it is not designed for low-entropy secrets such as passwords.

today: RFC 5869 is an Informational RFC and, per the unit metadata, no other RFC obsoletes or updates it. The text says HKDF was already used in IKEv2, PANA and EAP-AKA when it was published, and it remains the general specification of this key derivation function.

sections.title: Why Protocols Need a Key Derivation Function
sections.content:
A key derivation function (KDF) takes some source of initial keying material and derives from it one or more cryptographically strong secret keys. RFC 5869 specifies a simple KDF built on HMAC, named HKDF. The RFC notes that HKDF is already used in several IETF protocols, including IKEv2, PANA and EAP-AKA.

The purpose of the document is to describe the KDF in a general way so that future protocols can adopt it, and to discourage the proliferation of multiple KDF mechanisms. The authors state plainly that it is not a call to change existing protocols and does not update any specification that already uses this KDF.

HKDF follows the extract-then-expand paradigm: the KDF logically consists of two modules. The first stage extracts a fixed-length pseudorandom key from the input; the second stage expands that key into the outputs the protocol needs. The RFC notes that some other KDF specifications only cover the second stage, or do not separate the two stages, which often leads to design shortcomings.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol that starts with one secret often needs many keys. HKDF is a shared, tested way to produce them, so no new protocol has to invent its own method. It does not change protocols that already use a different method.

sections.title: Step 1: Extract
sections.content:
Extract takes an optional salt and the input keying material (IKM) and computes PRK = HMAC-Hash(salt, IKM). The output is a pseudorandom key (PRK) of HashLen octets, where HashLen is the output length of the chosen hash function. The RFC points out an easy trap: in this step the IKM is the HMAC input, not the HMAC key.

The salt is optional. When no salt is provided, it is set to a string of HashLen zeros. The goal of Extract is to concentrate the possibly dispersed entropy of the input keying material into a short but cryptographically strong key, even when an attacker has some partial knowledge or partial control of the input.
sections.plainLanguage: First you mix the raw secret with an optional salt value. The result is one short key of fixed length, even when the raw secret was uneven or partly known to an attacker.

sections.title: Step 2: Expand
sections.content:
Expand takes the PRK (at least HashLen octets, usually the Extract output), an optional info string and a desired length L in octets, which must be no more than 255*HashLen. It builds blocks of hash-sized output: T(0) is the empty string, and each block is T(i) = HMAC-Hash(PRK, T(i-1) | info | i), where i is a single-octet counter (0x01, 0x02, and so on). The output keying material (OKM) is the first L octets of the concatenated blocks.

The counter octet caps the output at 255 blocks. When the input is already a good pseudorandom key, Extract is not necessary and Expand can be used alone.
sections.plainLanguage: Then you stretch that fixed key into a stream of output bytes, adding a label that says what the keys are for. You cut off as many bytes as you asked for, up to the protocol's limit.

sections.title: Using Salt, Info and the Two Stages Well
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC is a set of guiding principles for users.

Salt. HKDF is defined to work with and without a salt so that it still fits applications where none is available, but the RFC stresses that using a salt adds significantly to strength: it keeps different uses of the hash function independent and strengthens the analysis behind the design. A salt is non-secret and can be reused. Ideally it is a random or pseudorandom string of length HashLen, but even a salt of lower quality or shorter length may still help, so designers are encouraged to provide one when they can. The salt must not be chosen or manipulated by an attacker; for example, in IKE the salt comes from nonces that are authenticated as part of the Diffie-Hellman exchange.

Info. The info input is optional but often of great importance. It binds the derived key material to application- and context-specific information, such as a protocol number, algorithm identifiers or user identities, so that the same input keying material used in different contexts does not yield the same keys. The one technical requirement is that info be independent of the IKM.

When to skip Extract. If the input is already a cryptographically strong key, one can skip Extract and use the IKM directly to key HMAC in Expand. The RFC makes one exception: if the IKM is a Diffie-Hellman value, Extract SHOULD NOT be skipped, because g^{xy} is not a uniformly random or pseudorandom string. Using the PRK directly as the output when L is no more than HashLen is NOT RECOMMENDED, because that would omit info from the derivation.
sections.plainLanguage: A salt is a non-secret random value that makes each run of the recipe come out differently, and it can be reused safely. The info label says what the keys are for, so the same secret never yields the same key in two different contexts. Skip the first step only when the input is already a strong key; a raw Diffie-Hellman value never qualifies.

sections.title: What HKDF Is Not For
sections.content:
The RFC lists intended applications: building pseudorandom generators from imperfect sources of randomness, generating keys from weak entropy sources such as system events or keystrokes, deriving keys from a shared Diffie-Hellman value in a key-agreement protocol, deriving symmetric keys in hybrid public-key encryption, and key derivation for key-wrapping mechanisms.

It also states a significant limitation. HKDF is not meant for deriving keys from a low-entropy source such as a user's password. The Extract step can concentrate existing entropy but cannot amplify it. Password-based KDFs aim to slow down dictionary attacks with two ingredients: a salt, and an intentional slowdown of the computation. HKDF accepts salt naturally, but a slowing-down mechanism is not part of the specification. Applications after a password-based KDF should consider whether PKCS #5 (RFC 2898) meets their needs better.

The security discussion is deliberately short and defers to the published HKDF paper. The analysis does not imply absolute security of any scheme: it depends heavily on the strength of the underlying hash function and on modeling choices, but it serves as a strong indication of the correct structure of the design.
sections.plainLanguage: HKDF can stretch a good secret into many keys, but it cannot make a weak secret strong. A short, easy password stays easy to guess no matter how it is mixed, so password-based systems need a slower method such as PKCS #5.

sections.title: Test Vectors for Implementers
sections.content:
Appendix A gives seven test cases so that implementers can check their code against known answers. They cover the SHA-256 and SHA-1 hash functions, short and long inputs and outputs, zero-length salt and info, and one case where the salt is not provided and defaults to HashLen zero octets.

For example, the first SHA-256 case uses a 22-octet IKM, a 13-octet salt, a 10-octet info and L = 42, and yields a 32-octet PRK and a 42-octet OKM.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is a set of practice problems with the answers included. You can run them against your own implementation to confirm it produces the same keys.

viz.caption: THE HKDF FORMULAS FROM RFC 5869, SECTIONS 2.2 AND 2.3

data.title: HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand
data.code:
PRK = HMAC-Hash(salt, IKM)

N = ceil(L/HashLen)
T(0) = empty string (zero length)
T(1) = HMAC-Hash(PRK, T(0) | info | 0x01)
T(2) = HMAC-Hash(PRK, T(1) | info | 0x02)
...
OKM = first L octets of T(1) | T(2) | ... | T(N)

viz.caption: THE TWO STAGES, FROM INPUT KEYING MATERIAL TO OUTPUT KEYS
